cands.name: Brian Burley

money.note: Individuals gave $64,623; PAC money $0; candidate's own money $186,000. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Republican candidate for California's 42nd Congressional District in 2026. Trustee on the Huntington Beach City School District board, elected 2024. Owns an information technology consulting company. Holds USC degrees in political economy and public policy. Past member of the Orange County Republican Central Committee.
cands.gaps: We could not find where Brian Burley was born or the year he moved to California. We found no record of his votes or actions on the Huntington Beach school board. We found no stated positions from him on data centers, development, growth, land ownership, guns, abortion or school choice. He did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. His campaign site gives general themes such as tax relief but no specific policies. We found no documented controversies, foreign ties or notable endorsements; Ballotpedia lists only two informal social-media voter guides.

cands.bio: Democratic U.S. Representative for California's 42nd District since January 2023. Former Mayor of Long Beach (2014–2022), city council member (2009–2014) and vice-mayor. Previously a professor of public policy and communications at USC, Cal State Long Beach and Long Beach City College. Born in Lima, Peru.

endorsements.text: For the 2026 race, endorsed by the Democratic Party of California, the California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO), the California Teachers Association, Sierra Club Angeles Chapter, California Environmental Voters, Equality California and YIMBY Action, among others listed on Ballotpedia.

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions or actions by Garcia on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land purchases, abortion, school choice or teacher pay, or police pay and pensions. His Ballotpedia profile says he did not complete its 2022, 2024 or 2026 candidate surveys. We could not confirm where he grew up or when he moved to California. No controversies or foreign ties appeared in the pages we had.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

qual.background: Assemblymember since December 2024, after eight years on the Etiwanda School District board (including a term as board president), with about 20 years as a teacher and school administrator and a USC master's in public policy.
qual.why: He has prior legislative service in the Assembly and local elected office, plus a public policy degree. His school administration work adds budget-related experience, but the pages don't document a budget or law career in detail.
qual.label: He has prior legislative service in the Assembly and local elected office, plus a public policy degree. His school administration work adds budget-related experience, but the pages don't document a budget or law career in detail.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: Says he is committed to fully funding schools and investing in classrooms, and calls strengthening public education a priority. This is a funding pledge, and the page does not mention vouchers, charters or teacher raises.

clean-money.evidence: Says he is fighting corporate monopolies, investor-owned utilities and billionaires, and standing up for people 'not the powerful special interests.' He does not pledge to refuse any specific kind of donation.

workers-first.evidence: Voted Nay on the Laken Riley Act, which requires DHS to detain certain unauthorized immigrants arrested for burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting. The bill passed the House 263-156 and was signed into law.

land_positions.quote_or_summary: His 2022 campaign website said: 'We must expand affordable and accessible housing across the United States,' and that Congress should fund significant housing development in American cities, especially along public transit and urban job centers.

controversies.text: Federal records show $7,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; 1 trip paid for by the American Israel Education Foundation, AIPAC's affiliate; 1 staff trip paid for by that foundation.
